description: We’re a team of innovators passionate about solving real-world problems through space technology. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're exploring SlopePulse, a solution using NASA satellite data to help identify areas needing inspection after heavy rainfall. We welcome teammates skilled in software development, Earth science, data analysis, UI/UX, and creative problem-solving. Join us to transform space data into meaningful action!
summary: TriageSAR helps road agencies decide where to inspect after an earthquake. We developed an open-source web application that turns NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations into an evidence-ranked road inspection queue. It converts real interferometric data into relative line-of-sight ground motion, flags weak or unusable measurements, identifies local deformation zones, and intersects them with OpenStreetMap roads. Each priority includes its contributing factors, observation dates, data quality and source provenance. Five real earthquake case studies demonstrate both populated queues and honest empty results when usable observations reveal no qualifying targets. A daily workflow checks for new NISAR coverage and publishes validated additions. TriageSAR addresses “Dancing with the SARs” by making complex radar data understandable and actionable while preserving uncertainty. It supports human inspection planning; it does not diagnose structural damage or certify roads as safe.
details:
Purpose and intended impact

TriageSAR supports road agencies and emergency planners who need to decide where to send inspection teams after an earthquake. It connects satellite evidence of ground motion with mapped roads and explains each road segment's position in the inspection queue. The public application is available at https://triagesar.devdragons.lk/ and the source code is open under Apache-2.0.

How it works

The scientific input is a real NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Unwrapped Interferogram (GUNW), discovered through the Alaska Satellite Facility catalogue. We read the study-area window of the HDF5 product and preserve source metadata and file checksums. Unwrapped phase becomes relative line-of-sight range change using the wavelength in the product metadata.

A transparent quality gate classifies pixels as VALID, CAUTION or EXCLUDED using coherence, connected components and the product mask. Excluded observations remain gaps and appear as hatching. For screening, a local plane fitted within each unwrapped region separates local motion from broad motion shared by the surrounding area. Contiguous areas must pass the configured motion threshold and minimum area before they become deformation zones.

The application intersects those zones with OpenStreetMap roads. A deterministic weighted score combines displacement magnitude, overlap extent, valid-observation fraction, coherence, proximity and road class. Evidence panels show the factor contributions, along-road profiles, acquisition dates and source provenance. Weight perturbation tests indicate whether the ranking is stable. No machine-learning or language model determines the scientific results or inspection ranking.

What the released application demonstrates

Five real NISAR case studies cover Venezuela, Japan, Panama, Indonesia and Mexico with the same analysis settings. Kumamoto produces 16 deformation zones and 936 ranked road-segment entries, with an explicit unstable-ranking warning. Other cases demonstrate empty queues and limited usable coverage. An empty queue means no qualifying targets were identified in the usable observations, not that roads are undamaged.

A daily workflow checks the USGS earthquake catalogue and ASF for newly available NISAR observations. It prepares new case studies, verifies checksums and runs science/API tests before publishing additions. The first automatic run added the Puerto Madero, Mexico case study. The interface includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation and text tables for access without using the map.

Tools and creative contribution

We use Python, NumPy, SciPy, h5py, Rasterio, pyproj, Shapely, Pydantic and FastAPI for the scientific pipeline and API. React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, TanStack Query and Vite provide the web interface. GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages build and publish the release. Tests use pytest, Vitest and Playwright. Our contribution is an auditable decision layer: infrastructure priorities accompanied by uncertainty, the reasoning behind each score, and traceable observations.

Limitations and next steps

The measurements describe one radar viewing direction and remain relative. The current pipeline applies no ionospheric, tropospheric or solid-Earth-tide corrections. Some source products are provisional, road inventories may be incomplete, and screening thresholds have not been calibrated against field inspections. TriageSAR supports human investigation and does not diagnose structural damage, predict casualties or certify safety. Next steps include field evaluation, atmospheric corrections, additional viewing geometries and authoritative infrastructure inventories.

Disclosure of Super Intelligence use

The team used Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to assist with software development, testing, documentation and submission wording. Scientific observations come from the cited NISAR products and other public datasets, not from generative models. Synthetic data exist only for clearly labelled automated tests and are excluded from the public case studies. The project screenshots are captures of the working application.
